(a) Findings.—Congress makes the following findings:
        (1) Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) serve Department of Defense intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and combat missions. 
        (2) Operational reliability of unmanned aerial systems continues to improve, and development and fielding of so-called sense-and-avoid technology should continue in order to provide unmanned aerial systems with an appropriate level of safety. 
        (3) Unmanned aerial vehicles have the potential to support the Nation’s homeland defense mission, border security mission, and natural disaster recovery efforts.  
    (b) Reports.—
        (1) DOD report.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the relevant congressional committees a report on the actions of the Department of Defense to develop standards for the testing and operation of unmanned aerial vehicles in the National Airspace System. 
        (2) FAA report.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration shall submit to the relevant congressional committees a report on progress in developing a policy for testing and a plan for achieving wider access by unmanned aerial vehicles that are appropriately equipped to operate in the National Airspace System 
        (3) Relevant congressional committee.—For the purposes of this subsection, the relevant congressional committees are the following:
            (A) The Committee on Armed Services, the Committee on Commerce, the Committee on Science and Transportation, and the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs of the Senate. 
            (B) The Committee on Armed Services, the Committee on Energy and Commerce, the Committee on Government Reform, and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that reports on developing standards and policy for UAV access to the National Airspace System imply a process involving outsiders. But the section contains only congressional findings and requirements that the Secretary of Defense and the FAA Administrator report to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. It does not require rulemaking, public comment, an advisory body, or consultation with states, industry, or the public, and it grants no right to sue.
fable.s: the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the relevant congressional committees a report on the actions of the Department of Defense to develop standards for the testing and operation of unmanned aerial vehicles in the National Airspace System.

qwen_block.w: This section requires federal agencies (the Department of Defense and the FAA) to submit reports to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation by outside parties. There is no requirement for consultation with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities before making a decision.
qwen_block.s: the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the relevant congressional committees a report on the actions of the Department of Defense to develop standards for the testing and operation of unmanned aerial vehicles in the National Airspace System.

opus.w: The section's only operative requirement is that the Secretary of Defense and the FAA Administrator report to congressional committees. Congress and its committees are inside the federal government, so this is not participation. The mention of developing standards and policy might suggest outside involvement, but nothing here requires rulemaking, public comment, or consultation with anyone outside the federal government.
opus.s: the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the relevant congressional committees a report on the actions of the Department of Defense to develop standards for the testing and operation of unmanned aerial vehicles in the National Airspace System.
opus.b: **Step 1 (brief analysis):** You might be tempted to read this as participation because it mentions developing "standards" and a "policy for testing," and it requires formal reports to several committees. That reading doesn't hold up. The only actors are the Secretary of Defense, the FAA Administrator, and congressional committees, and all of them are inside the federal government. The section requires no rulemaking, comment period, hearing, outside advisory body, or consultation with non-federal parties.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary of Defense and the FAA Administrator to submit reports to congressional committees. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is intra-governmental coordination, not participation by outside parties. There is no mention of public comment periods, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with states or the public.
qwen_chat.s: the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the relevant congressional committees a report on the actions of the Department of Defense to develop standards for the testing and operation of unmanned aerial vehicles in the National Airspace System.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the reports concern policy development (standards for UAVs), the process implicitly involves public input or that the reports themselves constitute a form of public engagement. However, the text explicitly states that the reports are submitted to "relevant congressional committees." Congress is part of the federal government. Therefore, this is intra-governmental reporting, not participation by outside parties.
